title: How many strings are enough
summary: He wants sixteen strings and distrusts doubling.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I was at a scoring session in New York, I think I mentioned to you the other day, I was just sitting in the studio listening, last January, and at one point they did have a th piece orchestra with eleven strings plus three trumpets, three 'bones, three french horns, tuba, full rhythm section, an extra keyboard and a couple of percussionists, and obviously that made all the difference in the world in the way it came off.
Sure; like the combination we used on Mickey One. That was all done there. They didn't start that stuff until later.
It's a good workable combination, I think, you have enough of everything to be able to do whatever
Not enough strings is the problem there.
What do you prefer, sixteen strings or twenty strings?
You should have sixteen fiddles and at least four violas and four cellos; at least that. Even that is not enough, you should have sixteen strings, eight each.
They way they had it was eleven strings, four first violins, three second violins--
I find that gets a little weak.
The arranger is Mike Aben (phonetic spelling), and what he did a lot of the time was he would be doubling the strings with, say flute and soprano sax just to bolster the sound a little bit.
If you do it at short stretches it comes out. For eight bars I think it's cool; if you do it for much longer I think it--

It gets a very special sound right away, because I tried doubling it with accordion or organ too when I get little ones like that. Accordion is a little less objectionable than flute and yet it takes the edge off the fiddle is what it does.

I heard an album that Johnny Mandel wrote about twenty years ago for David Allyn and I was with David Allyn when I heard it, and he was saying, do you hear the organ? Apparently Johnny used organ in the same way you mentioned, to bolster the strings and it was so subtly done that I really had to strain to catch it at all.
